item.title: - What fetters the world? What leads the world? By abandoning what thing Are all fetters cut? - Delight fetters the world, Seeking leads the…
item.description:
- What fetters the world?
What leads the world?
By abandoning what thing
Are all fetters cut?
- Delight fetters the world,
Seeking leads the world,
By abandoning craving,
All fetters are cut.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.65

item.title: “‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is ignorance? And to what extent is one called ignorant?” - “Here, monk, an untaught ordinary…
item.description:
“‘Ignorance, ignorance,’ venerable sir, is said. What, venerable sir, is ignorance? And to what extent is one called ignorant?” - “Here, monk, an untaught ordinary person does not know as it actually is: ‘Form is subject to origination’ as form is subject to origination; he does not know as it actually is: ‘Form is subject to cessation’ as form is subject to cessation; he does not know as it actually is: ‘Form is subject to origination and cessation’ as form is subject to origination and cessation. This, monk, is called ignorance. And to that extent one is called ignorant.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.126

item.title: - What gives birth to a person? What always runs about? What undergoes rebirth? What does a person fear? - Craving gives birth to a…
item.description:
- What gives birth to a person?
What always runs about?
What undergoes rebirth?
What does a person fear?
- Craving gives birth to a person,
The mind itself always runs about,
Beings undergo rebirth,
Suffering is what a person fears.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.55

item.title: “Deep, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and deep indeed is its definition. It is because of not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that beings…
item.description:
“Deep, Ānanda, is this dependent origination, and deep indeed is its definition. It is because of not understanding, not penetrating this Dhamma, Ānanda, that beings are tangled like a ball of thread, covered with blight, like muñja grass, like bulrushes, unable to escape from the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realm, saṃsāra. Ānanda, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are clung to — craving increases. With craving as condition, existence comes to be. With existence as condition, birth comes to be. With birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair arise. Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering. Just as, Ānanda, a great tree, having its roots that extend downward and laterally, all those roots convey the sap upwards — that great tree, being nourished and sustained in such a way, would stand for a long time. So too, Ānanda, one who dwells seeing gratification in things that are clung to — craving increases. With craving as condition, clinging comes to be … Such is the origination of this whole mass of suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.60

item.title: “And how, monks, does a monk dwell ‘as below, so above; as above, so below’? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this body from the soles…
item.description:
“And how, monks, does a monk dwell ‘as below, so above; as above, so below’? Here, monks, a monk contemplates this body from the soles of the feet upward, from the top of the head downward, enclosed by skin and full of various impurities: ‘There are in this body: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, diaphragm, spleen, lungs, intestines, intestinal mesentery, stomach, feces, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, skin oil, saliva, snot, synovial fluid, urine.’ Thus, monks, a monk dwells ‘as below, so above; as above, so below.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 51.20

item.title: “Monks, this body is subject to destruction, consciousness is subject to vanishing, all attachments are impermanent, suffering, subject to change. Knowing the body’s destruction, And…
item.description:
“Monks, this body is subject to destruction, consciousness is subject to vanishing, all attachments are impermanent, suffering, subject to change.

Knowing the body’s destruction,
And that consciousness must vanish,
Seeing the peril in attachments,
Understanding birth and death —

Having attained the supreme peace,
The mind is well-developed,
He simply bides his time.”

From: Itivuttaka 77

item.title: “And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it…
item.description:
“And when, monks, the mind is freed from these five defilements — sensual desire, ill-will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, doubt — then it becomes malleable, wieldy, radiant, not brittle, properly concentrated for the destruction of the defilements. Regarding whatever state is to be directly known, the mind inclines to direct knowledge, and in each case he attains the ability and capacity to realize that state.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.23
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, just as a forest deer, walking in the forest, walks confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, lies down confidently. Why is that? Because it has…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a forest deer, walking in the forest, walks confidently, stands confidently, sits confidently, lies down confidently. Why is that? Because it has escaped the hunter’s reach. So too, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. Monks, that monk is called one who has blinded Māra, who has destroyed his track, who has escaped the sight of Māra.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 26 – Ariyapariyesanāsutta

item.title: Who has crossed this mud, Crushed the thorn of sensuality, Attained the destruction of delusion — Such a monk, Does not feel pleasure or pain!
item.description:
Who has crossed this mud,
Crushed the thorn of sensuality,
Attained the destruction of delusion —
Such a monk,
Does not feel pleasure or pain!

From: Udana 3.2

item.title: Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One: How can one cross the flood, Steadfast and persevering day and…
item.description:
Standing to one side, the deity Candana recited this verse to the Blessed One:
How can one cross the flood,
Steadfast and persevering day and night?
Without stalling, without clinging —
Who does not sink in the abyss?

(The Blessed One):
One who always has virtue,
Wisdom, and is well-concentrated,
With aroused energy and strength —
That one crosses the hard-to-cross flood.
One who has abandoned perception of lust,
Who has crossed beyond the fetter of form,
Who has destroyed delight and craving for existence —
That one does not sink in the abyss.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.15
📖 Read this sutta
